reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours of Soft Tissue and Bone
clinicalPearls: One of the commonest adult soft-tissue sarcomas, comprising biologically distinct subtypes with very different behaviour
Well-differentiated and dedifferentiated liposarcomas characteristically arise in the retroperitoneum and deep extremities and share amplification of the 12q region with MDM2 and CDK4 overexpression
Well-differentiated liposarcoma (atypical lipomatous tumour in the limbs) does not metastasise but recurs locally, whereas dedifferentiation confers metastatic potential
Myxoid liposarcoma affects younger adults, favours the deep soft tissue of the extremities, and is defined by a FUS-DDIT3 (or rarely EWSR1-DDIT3) fusion
Myxoid liposarcoma has a distinctive tendency to metastasise to unusual soft-tissue and bony sites rather than lung, so staging should look beyond the chest
Pleomorphic liposarcoma is a rare, high-grade, genetically complex tumour with aggressive behaviour
MDM2 amplification testing by FISH reliably separates well-differentiated/dedifferentiated liposarcoma from benign lipomatous lesions
Wide surgical excision is the cornerstone of treatment, with radiotherapy and chemotherapy used selectively according to subtype and risk
reference.pathophysiology: Liposarcoma encompasses several distinct entities. Well-differentiated and dedifferentiated liposarcomas are driven by supernumerary ring or giant marker chromosomes containing amplified 12q13-15 material, leading to overexpression of MDM2 and CDK4 that inactivates p53-mediated control and drives the cell cycle; dedifferentiation represents progression to a non-lipogenic high-grade component. Myxoid liposarcoma is a translocation-associated tumour defined by a FUS-DDIT3 fusion gene that produces an aberrant transcription factor impairing adipocytic differentiation. Pleomorphic liposarcoma, by contrast, has a complex, unstable karyotype without a defining recurrent alteration, explaining its high-grade, aggressive phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Myxofibrosarcoma and other myxoid soft-tissue tumours
Retroperitoneal fibrosis or benign fatty proliferation
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI of the primary site to characterise fatty and non-fatty components and define resectability
Chest CT for pulmonary metastases in higher-grade subtypes
Whole-body and spinal MRI for myxoid liposarcoma given its atypical metastatic pattern
Core biopsy targeting non-fatty or enhancing areas to capture any dedifferentiated component
MDM2 (and CDK4) amplification testing by FISH or immunohistochemistry
Molecular testing for DDIT3 rearrangement when myxoid liposarcoma is suspected
redFlags: A large, deep, or retroperitoneal fatty mass with non-fatty enhancing areas suggesting dedifferentiation
Rapid enlargement or new pain in a previously indolent lipomatous lesion
Neurological, bony, or soft-tissue symptoms suggesting atypical metastases from myxoid liposarcoma
Recurrent retroperitoneal disease compromising adjacent organs
reference.prognosis: Prognosis varies markedly by subtype, grade, size, and site: well-differentiated tumours have an excellent survival but recur locally, retroperitoneal dedifferentiated disease carries a high recurrence risk, myxoid tumours have an intermediate course dependent on round-cell content, and pleomorphic liposarcoma has the poorest outlook.
pitfalls: Mistaking a well-differentiated liposarcoma for a benign lipoma without MDM2 testing
Sampling only the fatty component and missing a coexisting dedifferentiated area on biopsy
Staging myxoid liposarcoma with chest imaging alone and overlooking extrapulmonary metastases
Underestimating the local recurrence risk of retroperitoneal disease and the need for meticulous margins
Applying a single management approach across the biologically diverse subtypes
